paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach opens with a principle: what happened in the Torah is not a commemoration but repeats every year, as the geulah returns each Nisan and Kabbalas HaTorah each Shavuos. So the creation of the world repeats each Rosh Hashanah. The Mishnah in Avos counts ten utterances of creation, and each of the ten days creates another part of the world. That is why a year is called shanah, a repetition, as in the dream repeated to Pharaoh.

blocks.heading: Malchus, and why it is a day of judgment

paragraphs.text: Examining the Shemoneh Esrei of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the Mashgiach finds not one word calling it a day of judgment. Everything is Malchus, the coronation of Hashem: the Rosh Hashanah Amidah speaks of the holy King who reigns alone over the whole world. Judgment appears only in Zichronos of Musaf, which is not the character of the day's brachos.

Why, then, do the piyutim keep calling it the Day of Judgment? The Mashgiach brings his Rebbe's explanation. Each year Hashem creates a new world, and just as the Midrash tells of angels arguing whether Adam should be created, He now decides who will fit the purpose of His world and who would spoil and contaminate it. The day itself is meant for joy, which is why shuls sing marches like soldiers before their king; the judgment is its byproduct.

The Mashgiach adds that Hashem does not duplicate last year's world; He makes a better one. Newspapers, the streets and talking in shul may suggest decline, but the sefarim say the world improves each generation. Rebbe Reb Bunim taught that although earlier souls were greater, the innermost chamber of the heart grows better in every generation.

blocks.heading: Last year's mark is not enough

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya in Iggeres HaKodesh: the light that came down last Rosh Hashanah withdraws to its source, and with the tekios and the brachos a new, more sublime light descends, one the world has not had since Adam was created.

From this he answers a person who thinks: I survived last year, I am no worse now, so I will pass again. That is wrong, the Mashgiach says. Last year's mark fit last year; a better world demands promotion, and one who has not improved is failing. Therefore each Jew should make a cheshbon to improve, as the piyut calls to improve one's deeds, since Hashem improves even the heavens.

blocks.heading: Shabbos Shuvah: partner in the new creation

paragraphs.text: In the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah Hashem makes each Jew a partner in His creation, the Mashgiach explains, especially on Shabbos Shuvah, since keeping Shabbos testifies to creation. He asks for a Shabbos like never before, with a cheshbon hanefesh, Torah, good davening, and extra care in its laws, including the rabbinic ones and muktzeh.

Citing the Shelah, he says Shabbos itself should have pleasure from how it is kept, with joy. Hashem too should have oneg and nachas from His children; this is the one request in Tehillim, that Hashem should have pleasure from him.

blocks.heading: Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim of the heart

paragraphs.text: The ten days parallel the ten utterances, and the tenth, Yom Kippur, is the highest. Of the ten levels of holiness the tenth is the Kodesh HaKodashim, which only the Kohen Gadol enters, only on Yom Kippur. The Gemara says that when Jews do teshuvah their souls go in with him. Yom Kippur is the Kodesh HaKodashim of the calendar.

Every Jew is a miniature Beis HaMikdash, as the passuk in Yirmiyahu says, with a hidden chamber whose only desire is Hashem's will. The Rambam explains that one compelled until he says he wants does mean it, since that will lies in every heart. On Yom Kippur one should dig until he reaches that point.
Noting that five days remain, with Shabbos Shuvah and Yom Kippur ahead, the Mashgiach asks that people daven for Klal Yisrael and that all Jews do teshuvah together with the new world.
